comments.author: @roberts4058
comments.text:
Great documentary! A couple of special places in Romania are also worth mentioning:

1.The Retezat Mountains, home to Bucura Lake, the largest glacial lake in Romania, and the surreal alpine landscapes you can admire from Peleaga Peak.
2.The Apuseni Mountains, famous for their spectacular caves, such as Scărișoara Ice Cave and Bear's Cave, as well as their beautiful karst landscapes, gorges, forests and traditional mountain villages.
3.The picturesque Cheile Nerei–Beușnița National Park, with its turquoise-blue Ochiul Beiului spring, beautiful waterfalls and the incredible green-blue waters of Lacul Dracului.
4.I would also include my favorite historic place, Băile Herculane, an old spa town surrounded by mountains. It is worth visiting not only for its beautiful historic architecture, but also for its thermal waters and the many hiking trails in the surrounding Cerna Mountains.
5.If you're into hiking, the Rodnei Mountains should definitely be high on your list. They offer some of the most impressive alpine scenery in Romania, with dramatic ridges, glacial lakes and wide mountain valleys. The area is also home to the spectacular Horses' Waterfall (Cascada Cailor), one of Romania's most famous waterfalls. For hikers, routes around Pietrosul Rodnei, the highest peak of the range, offer incredible panoramic views and a real taste of Romania's wild Carpathian landscape.
6.Dobrogea deserves a special mention as well, as it offers some of the most unusual landscapes in Romania. The ancient Măcin Mountains, among the oldest mountain formations in the country, have a completely different character from the Carpathians, with rocky ridges, open steppe landscapes and beautiful hiking trails. The region also offers the spectacular limestone scenery of Cheile Dobrogei, the medieval Enisala Fortress overlooking Lake Razim, and a fascinating mixture of wetlands, rocky hills and wild landscapes stretching towards the Black Sea and the Danube Delta.
7.The Ceahlău Mountains are another magical part of Romania, famous for their dramatic rock formations, legends and the beautiful Duruitoarea Waterfall. Ceahlău is also associated with a fascinating phenomenon known as the "Ceahlău Pyramid." Around early August, under the right conditions and at sunrise, the shadows cast by the mountain peaks can create the appearance of a huge pyramid on the horizon. Whether you visit for the phenomenon, the legends or simply the scenery, watching the sunrise from Ceahlău is an unforgettable experience.
8.And finally, the Piatra Craiului Mountains and the landscapes around "Amfiteatrul Transilvania" are among my favorite views in the country. The long, spectacular limestone ridge rising above the green valleys creates scenery that, in some places, feels like a smaller Romanian answer to the dramatic landscapes of Yosemite. Early in the morning, if you're lucky, you may even spot chamois on the rocky slopes. The combination of sharp limestone peaks, forests, traditional villages and open meadows makes this part of Transylvania particularly beautiful.

Romania has so much more to offer beyond its most famous destinations. From the high alpine landscapes of Retezat and Rodnei to the ancient Măcin Mountains, the caves of Apuseni, the turquoise waters of Nerei, the legends of Ceahlău and the limestone walls of Piatra Craiului, the diversity of landscapes within such a relatively small country is remarkable.

You are mistaken—though I know this misconception is perpetuated by many historians who are out of touch with reality and common sense.
Dacia—present-day Romania—was not conquered by the Roman Empire in the way some imagine; Rome occupied only about 24–25% of Dacia's total territory. Throughout that time, Dacians from the unoccupied, free territories constantly attacked Roman forts, eventually forcing Rome to withdraw all its legions from Dacia after 160–170 years.
The language spoken in Romania is not due to Rome; how could a people possibly abandon their own language under an occupation covering only 25% of their territory for a period of 170 years?
How much of Britain did the Romans conquer? For how many centuries did Roman legions remain there?
How is it that the British did not abandon their language?
What about the Celtic tribes in present-day Spain? Or those in present-day France? The language spoken in Romania is not the result of the Roman Empire; the Dacians were not a savage people lacking their own culture and language.

I’m always proud to see the Transfăgărășan getting a mention in these travel documentaries…
My late father-in-law (Dr ing Aurel Ungur) was the person that suggested to Ceaușescu to build it as a tourist road, when he was the Secretary of State for Forestry and Agriculture back in the late 60s.
Ceaușescu rejected the proposal, so Aurel put the idea to the Military, and they convinced Ceaușescu it was a good idea.
Aurel mapped out the route on horseback and supervised the construction.
He was an awesome man, always campaigned against the destruction of the forests to his very last day, he passed away peacefully in 2020 at the age of 99 (and a half).
God bless him ❤

Plus că în munții și pădurile din Neamț (și nu numai) încă se nevoiesc pustnici cu viață duhovnicească înlată, sfântă aș putea spune.. exact la la Pateric.. Plus: Cetatea Neamț, Lacul Cuiejdel, Zimbrăria, Casa Memorială Ion Creangă, Piatra Neamț 'ul cu cu muzeul eneolitic cu cea mai veche civilizatie din Europa - Cucuteni, Barajul Bicaz, Muntele Ceahlău, Cheile Bicazului etc!
